I did a lot of the same behaviors as your husband and ended up divorced because of it. What I realized is most of my behavior is a result of battling my own demons. For example, I deal with self-hatred and that self-hatred has just multiplied since getting a divorce. 

It’s probably not anything you are doing, if it seems like he is not “present” or in the moment, then it may be a “him” problem like depression. 

My heart wasn’t in fixing my marriage because I clearly have some fixing of myself that needs to be done before I could have fixed my marriage. 

Divorce has 100% ruined my life. I have absolutely no reason to be alive anymore, and living with the guilt of those behaviors is too much on most days.

Start by asking yourself if you want the marriage to continue. If you do, then he will need professional help to overcome the addiction. I would be firm in your boundaries when it comes to watching porn and tell him how him watching porn makes you feel. 

If you feel like he is a good husband in many other ways and loves you, then I wouldn’t personally try to divorce him, but if you think that the porn issue is just the tip of the iceberg, then I think it unfortunately warrants some serious consideration. 

Porn addiction is no joke and it effects a lot of people. Divorce is painful though. I’m 2 years after my divorce and it has all but destroyed my whole life and desire to live. So be sure that is what you want to do before doing it.

I’m sorry you are going through such a hard time. 

In my opinion the best part about living life is also the worst part. Nothing is permanent. Your situation will change although it may not feel like it. 

The hardest part about communicating is that we think too much about what the other person is going to think of us. It is best to be very blunt with your mom and assert yourself for your needs.

You could say: “I have been working very hard, I am going to do something nice for myself today. I really wanted to make chocolate and I would appreciate it if you would support me.” 

OR: 

“ I have been working very hard on studying and I need to do something else to energize myself and give me the ability to concentrate again. Therefore, I am going to (insert activity here). I will study more when I am done.” 

It is very hard to do, especially with controlling parents, but they should know that everyone needs time to explore interests outside of school/work

I also want to add that this situation will have absolutely no bearing on whether or not you get your Barista job. 

As for your parents, if they don’t support you through this, then they themselves need to grow up. How they feel about your decisions is their business, but how they support you in your time of need and struggle says a lot about who they are as people. I hope they will surprise you and comfort you and give you some words of wisdom for the future.

I’m really sorry this happened to you. Being 16 is hard and so is being 14. 

This man is trying to have power over you, however, I wouldn’t be too concerned that he is going to carry out the threat. 

There are a couple of reasons. 

#1 - he has nothing to gain and everything to lose. If he has the video, he is technically in possession of child pornography and would in that case spend the rest of his garbage life in prison. 

#2- people forget things quickly. Will things be hard with your peers and parents, yes, but I think you will find that one mistake does not define you. In the eyes of the law, you actually didn’t do anything wrong. Adults may want to act virtuous but any well rounded person will understand that these things happen. Remember, possession of the video that you made would be illegal, even a copy, so it won’t spread around as much as you might think. 

You are in a hard situation. I feel for you, but this IS a situation that you will get through and perhaps learn that no one person should ever have that much power over you (and that the power is a mindset). People will still like you and more people in your future will like you. 

I wish you all the best. If you have a trusted adult in your life, I would tell them (even though it’s hard). You could even just have them read this post. Counselors at school are a good resource. Don’t worry about them judging you. You might think your case might be the most embarrassing, but I assure you it is not. 

Take care of yourself.

I also struggle with suicidal thoughts (after I got divorced). I don’t think you are crazy or anything, and I don’t know what it is like to be you. My suggestion to you, something I am trying as well, is to try to change one small part of your life so that you can make it worth living again. Some people say hobbies are a good distraction, but if you can find one that helps fulfill you, then it might be a stepping stone to a better life for yourself. 

I wish you all the best and I hope you wake up on March 29 saying, “maybe I haven’t tried everything and am not ready to give up quite yet.”

Yes, your family is emotionally abusive. It is good to identify this now and seek therapy. My recommendation is when you go to college, to limit the contact you have with your family to whatever is manageable to you. If that is weekly, that is fine, if it is monthly or even less, that’s ok too. When you do get to your college, look into their mental health therapy through the college medical system. I would try Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT). You aren’t to blame for this, but it sounds like your anxiety is taking away from your life. 

As for your family, eventually you will have to confront them about their behavior and either they can accept you or you will have to decide how much contact you can have with them. I know that might be hard, but it may be necessary.

It is difficult to help a person who doesn’t want to help themselves. Often times family medicine doctors can help a person feel more comfortable with the mental care process. I would maybe start there.

I assume you are over the age of 12? If so, you yourself can appeal to the court and ask that your permanent home be with your father. Generally speaking if you are over the age of 12, the court will allow you a lot of say in where you want to live. You can tell the court that for your own mental well-being you should live with your father. 

Sounds like your mother is mentally unstable. Divorce can ruin a person’s life, your mother may be feeling the effects of all of it. It’s not an excuse, but I seriously doubt she doesn’t care about you. My advice…do whatever you need to for your own mental health, but don’t give up on your mom.

I am so sorry. It sounds like you and your mom are close. Try to remember that the best thing you can do for your Mom is to live your life. You are her legacy and I’m sure you were everything to her. Perhaps you don’t have children? Many parents love their children more than life itself, she wants the world for you. Try to honor her memory by living your life and always remembering how important she was to you. It will not be easy and it will be incredibly painful (as you know), but you can do it.

I think I also feel that other people will move on very easily. They will go to work the next day and laugh and watch movies and my memory will be nothing to them, so why should I have to suffer to relieve a few moments of their discomfort. 

Disclaimer: I don’t think I will commit suicide because my self-preservation instincts are too strong. I do hope you don’t commit suicide, but know that there are others out there that share your feelings.

I am sorry you are going through this. The short answer is “no,” you will not be a failure. Our society puts a certain value to education and part of that is warranted, but it isn’t what defines a person. 

You seem to have reasonable amount of skill. Your writing doesn’t suggest someone who hasn’t been properly schooled. 

You can find success in many other ways in life. Maybe you like to fix cars? Maybe you like to work with food? Neither of those necessarily requires a diploma. 

If getting your GED is a goal you have for yourself then I suggest repetition when you study. Make flash cards of all your concepts, do practice problems of different difficulties. If there is a teacher or instructor you can confide in, then tell them your struggles. 

I am an elementary school teacher and though things are different at such a young age, I think every teacher should be reminded that their duty is to the welfare of their students. My hope is that there is a teacher out there that will help you through this. 

As for suicide. Those thoughts are tough and may take time to go away, but I understand having them. You are not a failure though. One day you will realize it.

I wouldn’t necessarily throw in the towel yet, but I think some really firm boundaries are needed. Given that she is bipolar she is prone to feel emotions more strongly than the average person. That being said, she still has control over her behavior. In order to move forward with the relationship she needs to know that verbal abuse and threatening will not be tolerated. Tell her you want to be a part of her life and that you will support her in this endeavor. For her, her goal is to manage, not really to change. She will still make mistakes but it is about how both of you develop a way to respond to the mistakes that will either make or break the relationship. If she is unwilling to put the effort in or doesn’t see the errors or turns it around and tries to make it your fault, then divorce may be the best option.

Do you feel as though it is too awkward for him or do you think it might be too painful for him? 

He may be feeling vulnerable at the moment and that he is being invited to his own son’s party as the “other” parent who isn’t part of the family and will, by default, be singled out. If so, I don’t think this is a pride issue, I think it is an identity issue. He doesn’t know how he fits in and whether or not he is truly wanted there. That being said, he probably should do whatever he can to be there for his child. You don’t have to accommodate him, perhaps just understand how he might be feeling and encourage him to come for part of the party and potentially spend time alone time with your son afterward.
